arc: hook (a prompt typed into a terminal, agent output streaming back to a device code) → feature (wallet consent screen with a 3D code tile, Continue pressed) → conversation (agent proposes an itinerary change and a $180 charge in chat, user says yes) → feature (spend request banner on a phone lock screen) → workflow (approval sheet, Face ID scan, receipt) → logo (the Link mark lands)

scenes.title: Terminal: prompt typed, skill URL pasted, agent output streams to a device code
scenes.summary: Dark green field, monospace. A 50px white prompt reads '❯ install link using' typing on an uneven rhythm, then 'https://link.com/skill.md' pastes in on a second line in green and cools to white while the whole prompt slowly zooms from 0.78 to 1. The prompt lifts and fades, a framed card scales up behind, and 30px agent output streams in line by line with square bullet glyphs: 'I'll help you set up your link account to use for a wallet', 'install link-cli / L Done', 'Starting connection... / L Calling link auth-start.', then a Visit block with 'https://link.com/device?code=apple-grape-orange' and the passphrase 'apple-grape-orange'. It settles on 'Waiting for approval...' whose dots cycle on a nine frame loop, and the whole block drifts up 2% over the hold.
scenes.build: Text is drawn into OffscreenCanvas textures and mounted as planes on an orthographic stage where 1 world unit is 100 design px (components/stage.ts), so a 1080 square is authored in top-left design coordinates. Typing is `revealLeft`, which scales a left-anchored plane's x and its texture `repeat.x` to the measured width of the typed prefix, driven by an explicit `keyFrames` array of per-character frames rather than a constant rate. Terminal lines are `richLine`, a canvas plane built from [text, colour] runs so one line can mix body grey and token green. The cycling dots reuse `revealLeft` against a pre-measured 'Waiting for approval' width plus N dot widths.
scenes.reuse: The strongest terminal-output shot in the catalog: borrow it for any 'install our CLI / connect our MCP server' opener. Swap the `lines` array (copy, colour runs, per-line entry frame) and the prompt strings, and re-tune `keyFrames` for a different command length. The irregular keystroke array is the part that makes it read as a person, so keep its shape. Don't keep the link.com URLs, the apple-grape-orange passphrase, or the Link green.

scenes.title: Wallet consent screen with a 3D code tile and a Continue press
scenes.summary: Cuts to white. An extruded, bevelled rounded-square tile in pale mint floats at the top, carrying a '</>' code glyph on its face, tilting and bobbing under two directional lights with a soft elliptical shadow beneath. 'Connect an agent' sits below in 46px Inter, then three icon rows stagger up: 'Make agentic purchases / Pay using your saved payment details.', 'Keep your payment details private / We'll generate a virtual card number for each purchase.', and 'Approve every spend request / Review and approve with biometric authentication.' A full width black Continue button presses at frame 46, scaling down 3%, then crossfades to a grey disabled state as the whole screen fades out.
scenes.build: The tile is a real THREE.ExtrudeGeometry from a hand-built rounded Shape with bevel, in MeshPhysicalMaterial with clearcoat and sheen, lit by key plus fill plus ambient, with a separate canvas plane for the glyph face and a radial-gradient canvas squashed on y for the shadow. Everything else is flat canvas planes on the same orthographic stage. Row icons are drawn from a `GLYPHS` table of small stroke routines inside a light circle. The button is two stacked planes (active and pressed) whose opacities cross over, so the disabled state is a crossfade rather than a redraw.
scenes.reuse: A permissions or consent screen for any product that asks for access: swap the three `rows` (title, two sub lines, glyph key) and the headline. The extruded clearcoat tile is a cheap way to get one 3D element into an otherwise flat UI shot and is worth lifting on its own. The two-plane button crossfade is reusable for any pressed-then-disabled control. Don't keep the Link wording about virtual card numbers.

scenes.title: Monospace agent chat with a glowing summary-of-changes card
scenes.summary: Back on dark green. A chat lays out right and left: the user asks 'Adjust my road trip itinerary to stay in New Orleans another night.' in a lighter bubble, the agent replies 'Found availability in your same room for another night and found a last-minute discount.' in a bordered dark bubble. A 560px summary card then drops in with a green outer glow and a green border, headed 'Summary of changes' with three ruled rows: 'Extra night +$210', 'Last minute discount -$30' and a bold 'Total charge $180'. The agent asks 'Would you like to confirm?', the card's glow breathes, and after a long beat a small 'Yes' bubble lands on the right. The chat pushes 6% towards the viewer and fades on the exit.
scenes.build: A `bubble()` helper measures the longest line in monospace, sizes a canvas plane to it plus padding, and draws a rounded rect with optional stroke and the lines at a fixed 38px leading. Layout is top-y plus a side flag, converted to a centre point from the measured width and height, so adding a message is one array entry. The summary card reserves a 24px transparent gutter so a canvas shadowBlur can bleed without clipping, and the glow 'breathes' by modulating the material opacity on `time`. Every item shares one entry curve plus a `pop` overshoot keyed off its own start frame.
scenes.reuse: Use it for any agent-proposes-then-human-confirms beat, which is the core shot of an approval or human-in-the-loop story. Swap the `items` array for your own messages and the summary card's `rows` for your own line items. The transparent-gutter trick for a glowing card and the measure-then-size bubble helper are both worth lifting. Don't keep the New Orleans itinerary or the $210/$30/$180 figures.

scenes.title: Phone lock screen lights up with a spend request banner
scenes.summary: A detailed phone stands centre frame on the dark green field: titanium band, black bezel, side buttons, dynamic island with a camera lens, a glass sheen and a soft double shadow. Its lock screen is a dark green gradient with two translucent ribbon curves, a status bar, a lock glyph, 'Thu Apr 2' and a large '11:58'. A notification banner drops into the lower third reading 'Approve spend request' over 'Triplo · $180' with 'now' on the right and the Link app icon rounded into a tile on the left, then lifts and scales 5% towards the viewer. The phone floats faintly throughout.
scenes.build: The whole device is components/phone.ts, shared with scene 5 so the two cut on an identical phone: `deviceFrame()` draws the hardware into one canvas and then uses `destination-out` to punch the screen out, so whatever plane sits behind shows through concentric corner radii (body 78, inset 20, screen 58). The app icon is a plain PNG plane with a `roundedMask()` canvas texture as its `alphaMap`, which is how a square source image gets a squircle without touching the file. The banner is a single canvas plane; its entry combines an eased drop with a `pop` overshoot and a separate later 'lift' interpolation.
scenes.reuse: Lift components/phone.ts wholesale any time you need a convincing phone that is not a flat screenshot; it is the best device mock in the catalog and the punch-out trick means you can put any screen behind it. Swap the banner's two lines and the icon for your own app. Note this scene is not standalone: it needs components/phone.ts, components/backdrop.ts and the app icon asset.

scenes.title: Approval sheet, Face ID scan and the receipt that lands
scenes.summary: The same phone, now showing a white app sheet. A circled code glyph sits above 'openclaw-jane wants to spend $180', over a grouped card with a Triplo merchant row (with an Inspect pill) and a 'Queen room / New Orleans / $180.00' row, then a 'Visa Credit / •••• 1234' row. Decline and a black Approve button sit at the bottom; Approve presses at frame 46. The screen dims green and a Face ID tile scales up, its green face outline pulsing while it scans, then at frame 122 the face fades as a ring sweeps clockwise from twelve o'clock and a tick draws itself left to right. Everything clears and the receipt fades up: the Triplo mark, 'Triplo', 'Mar 3, 2026, 1:34 PM', '$180', a bordered card with 'Status Approved' and 'Payment Visa Credit 1234', and an 'Agent openclaw-jane' row. The phone shrinks and fades before the cut.
scenes.build: The longest scene and effectively three screens in one timeline, sequenced by named frame constants (PRESS, DIM, SUCCESS, CLEAR, RECEIPT) with each group's opacity driven off them, so retiming is editing five numbers. The Face ID success ring is a THREE.RingGeometry whose `setDrawRange` is advanced by an interpolation, mirrored on x so it draws clockwise, which is a cheap stroke-dashoffset equivalent in Three.js. The tick uses `revealLeft` on a left-anchored canvas plane to wipe itself on. Rows are drawn at real px into canvas planes sized from the shared SCREEN box, so the layout follows the phone.
scenes.reuse: The reference for a biometric-approval or confirm-then-receipt beat. The RingGeometry draw-range progress ring and the wipe-on tick are self-contained and reusable for any success state. Swap the merchant, room, amount and card rows, and the agent name. Retime by moving the five frame constants. Not standalone: it shares components/phone.ts with scene 4.

scenes.title: Link mark lands centre frame and breathes
scenes.summary: A two second end card. The dark green field with no framed card, its dot grid glowing from two off-centre patches low and right. The Link wordmark fades up at 300x132 with a small overshoot, settles, then breathes by well under a percent for the rest of the hold.
scenes.build: A PNG on a plane sized in design px, with the shared `pop` overshoot curve multiplied by a slow sine on `time` so the hold is never frozen. The backdrop is called with `frame: false` and custom glow centres, which is the one knob that makes the end card read differently from the scenes before it despite being the same component.
scenes.reuse: A drop-in end card for any video: replace the PNG and set the plane's size to its real pixel dimensions. The pattern of reusing the backdrop with the frame off and the glow moved is the thing to copy, so the end card belongs to the film without repeating it. Don't keep the Link mark.
